claim: ABCG2 is an exporter-type ABC protein that can expel numerous chemically unrelated xeno- and endobiotics from cells.
source: ABCG2 is an exporter-type ABC protein that can expel numerous chemically unrelated xeno- and endobiotics from cells.
evidence: This is a general characterization of ABCG2 function, supported by established scientific knowledge about this transporter.

claim: When expressed in tumor cells or tumor stem cells, ABCG2 confers multidrug resistance, contributing to the failure of chemotherapy.
source: When expressed in tumor cells or tumor stem cells, ABCG2 confers multidrug resistance, contributing to the failure of chemotherapy.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about ABCG2's role in cancer drug resistance.

claim: The switch from the inward-facing (IF) to the outward-facing (OF) conformation of ABCG2 is induced by nucleotide binding.
source: Using the conformation-sensitive antibody 5D3, we show that the switch from the inward-facing (IF) to the outward-facing (OF) conformation of ABCG2 is induced by nucleotide binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using the 5D3 antibody presented in the manuscript.

claim: IF-OF transition is facilitated by substrates.
source: IF-OF transition is facilitated by substrates, and hindered by the inhibitor Ko143.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing substrate effects on conformational transitions.

claim: IF-OF transition is hindered by the inhibitor Ko143.
source: IF-OF transition is facilitated by substrates, and hindered by the inhibitor Ko143.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Ko143 effects on conformational transitions.

claim: The high-to-low affinity switch of the drug binding site coincides with the transition from the IF to the OF conformation.
source: Direct measurements of 5D3 and substrate binding to ABCG2 indicate that the high-to-low affinity switch of the drug binding site coincides with the transition from the IF to the OF conformation.
evidence: This is supported by direct experimental measurements of 5D3 and substrate binding presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low substrate binding persists in the post-hydrolysis state.
source: Low substrate binding persists in the post-hydrolysis state, supporting that dissociation of the ATP hydrolysis products is required to reset the high substrate affinity IF conformation of ABCG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on substrate binding in different conformational states.

claim: Dissociation of the ATP hydrolysis products is required to reset the high substrate affinity IF conformation of ABCG2.
source: Low substrate binding persists in the post-hydrolysis state, supporting that dissociation of the ATP hydrolysis products is required to reset the high substrate affinity IF conformation of ABCG2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that low substrate binding persists in the post-hydrolysis state.

claim: ABCG2 is also known as Breast Cancer Resistance Protein (BCRP), Mitoxantrone Resistance Protein (MXR), and Placenta-Specific ABC transporter (ABCP).
source: The human ABCG2 protein (also known as Breast Cancer Resistance Protein [BCRP], Mitoxantrone Resistance Protein [MXR], and Placenta-Specific ABC transporter [ABCP]) is a primary active transporter that belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein superfamily (Doyle et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established nomenclature supported by citation.

claim: ABCG2 is a primary active transporter that belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein superfamily.
source: The human ABCG2 protein (also known as Breast Cancer Resistance Protein [BCRP], Mitoxantrone Resistance Protein [MXR], and Placenta-Specific ABC transporter [ABCP]) is a primary active transporter that belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) protein superfamily (Doyle et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doyle et al., 1998.

claim: ABCG2 can expel chemotherapeutic drugs from cells.
source: ABCG2 can expel a large variety of chemically unrelated molecules, mainly hydrophobic or amphipathic compounds from cells, including chemotherapeutic drugs and toxic metabolic side-products such as pheophorbide A (Jonker et al., 2002), estrone-3-sulfate (E3S) (Suzuki et al., 2003), and uric acid (Woodward et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: ABCG2 can expel pheophorbide A from cells.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Jonker et al., 2002.

claim: ABCG2 is expressed in tissues with barrier functions including the blood-brain barrier, blood-testis barrier, intestine, liver, placenta, kidneys, and mammary glands.
source: ABCG2 is expressed in tissues with barrier functions including the blood-brain barrier, blood-testis barrier, intestine, liver, placenta, kidneys, and mammary glands (Doyle et al., 1998; Fetsch et al., 2006; van Herwaarden and Schinkel, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ABCG2 plays an important role in the absorption, distribution, elimination, and toxicity (ADME-Tox) of chemotherapeutic drugs.
source: Because of its tissue localization and its broad substrate spectrum, ABCG2 plays an important role in the absorption, distribution, elimination, and toxicity (ADME-Tox) of chemotherapeutic drugs used for the treatment of various diseases (Giacomini et al., 2013; Sarkadi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giacomini et al., 2013 and Sarkadi et al., 2006.

claim: The expression of ABCG2 in tumor tissues, especially in tumor stem cells or drug-tolerant persister cells, correlates with an unfavorable prognosis of tumor chemotherapy.
source: In addition, the expression of ABCG2 in tumor tissues, especially in the so-called tumor stem cells or drug-tolerant persister cells, correlates with an unfavorable prognosis of tumor chemotherapy (Ding et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ding et al., 2010.

claim: Genetic polymorphisms leading to decreased expression and/or impaired function of ABCG2 may result in various pathological conditions.
source: On the other hand, genetic polymorphisms leading to decreased expression and/or impaired function of ABCG2 may result in various pathological conditions (recently reviewed in Homolya, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Homolya, 2021.

claim: Genetic polymorphisms in ABCG2 can result in altered therapy responses.
source: These include altered therapy responses, drug-related toxic reactions, as well as hyperuricemia and gout (Ishikawa et al., 2013), since ABCG2 is also a key player of the intestinal uric acid elimination pathway (Woodward et al., 2009; Köttgen and Köttgen, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishikawa et al., 2013.

claim: Genetic polymorphisms in ABCG2 can result in drug-related toxic reactions.
source: These include altered therapy responses, drug-related toxic reactions, as well as hyperuricemia and gout (Ishikawa et al., 2013), since ABCG2 is also a key player of the intestinal uric acid elimination pathway (Woodward et al., 2009; Köttgen and Köttgen, 2021).

claim: ABCG2 is a 'half-transporter', consisting of an N-terminal nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), followed by a C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD).
source: ABCG2 is a 'half-transporter', consisting of an N-terminal nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), followed by a C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that form homodimers in the plasma membrane to obtain a functional transporter (Kage et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kage et al., 2002 and represents established structural knowledge.

claim: ABCG2 forms homodimers in the plasma membrane to obtain a functional transporter.
source: ABCG2 is a 'half-transporter', consisting of an N-terminal nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), followed by a C-terminal transmembrane domain (TMD) that form homodimers in the plasma membrane to obtain a functional transporter (Kage et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kage et al., 2002.

claim: In all ABC transporters, ATP is bound by the Walker A and B motifs of one NBD and by the signature sequence of the other NBD, resulting in a close interaction of the two NBDs, which is often referred to as 'sandwich-dimer'.
source: In all ABC transporters, ATP is bound by the Walker A and B motifs of one NBD and by the signature sequence of the other NBD, resulting in a close interaction of the two NBDs, which is often referred to as 'sandwich-dimer' (Locher, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Locher, 2009 and represents established knowledge about ABC transporter mechanism.

claim: In the absence of ATP, apo-ABCG2 adopts an inward-facing (IF) state, wherein the transmembrane cavity is open toward the cytosolic side.
source: In the absence of ATP, apo-ABCG2 adopts an inward-facing (IF) state, wherein the transmembrane cavity is open toward the cytosolic side, with the central four transmembrane helices (TH2, TH5, TH2′, and TH5′) forming a large drug-binding pocket (cavity 1) accessible for substrate binding (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The central four transmembrane helices (TH2, TH5, TH2′, and TH5′) form a large drug-binding pocket (cavity 1) accessible for substrate binding in the IF state.
source: In the absence of ATP, apo-ABCG2 adopts an inward-facing (IF) state, wherein the transmembrane cavity is open toward the cytosolic side, with the central four transmembrane helices (TH2, TH5, TH2′, and TH5′) forming a large drug-binding pocket (cavity 1) accessible for substrate binding (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ATP-bound ABCG2 is in an outward-facing (OF) state, allowing the release of substrates to the extracellular side.
source: ATP-bound ABCG2 is in an outward-facing (OF) state, allowing the release of substrates to the extracellular side (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IF structure contains two substrate-binding cavities: a large central cavity at the cytoplasmic side (cavity 1) and an additional cavity (cavity 2) located toward the extracellular part of ABCG2.
source: The IF structure contains two substrate-binding cavities: a large central cavity at the cytoplasmic side (cavity 1) and an additional cavity (cavity 2) located toward the extracellular part of ABCG2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The two cavities are separated by L554 and L555, which form a tight hydrophobic seal at the top of cavity 1, preventing the entry of substrates to cavity 2 in the IF conformation.
source: The two cavities are separated by L554 and L555, which form a tight hydrophobic seal at the top of cavity 1, preventing the entry of substrates to cavity 2 in the IF conformation (Taylor et al., 2017; Khunweeraphong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2017 and Khunweeraphong et al., 2017.

claim: The ATP-free IF state can be detected by the conformation-sensitive monoclonal antibody 5D3.
source: The ATP-free IF state can be detected by the conformation-sensitive monoclonal antibody 5D3 (Taylor et al., 2017), which recognizes two composite epitopes formed by extracellular loops (Figure 1C and E) that are disengaged in the OF state (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2017 and structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The 5D3 antibody recognizes two composite epitopes formed by extracellular loops that are disengaged in the OF state.
source: The ATP-free IF state can be detected by the conformation-sensitive monoclonal antibody 5D3 (Taylor et al., 2017), which recognizes two composite epitopes formed by extracellular loops (Figure 1C and E) that are disengaged in the OF state (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2017 and structural data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformer of the E211Q mutant ABCG2, cavity 1 is completely collapsed.
source: In the ATP-bound conformer of this mutant protein, cavity 1 is completely collapsed, the di-leucine gate is closed, while cavity 2 is open to the extracellular side of the plasma membrane (Manolaridis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manolaridis et al., 2018.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformer of the E211Q mutant ABCG2, the di-leucine gate is closed.
source: In the ATP-bound conformer of this mutant protein, cavity 1 is completely collapsed, the di-leucine gate is closed, while cavity 2 is open to the extracellular side of the plasma membrane (Manolaridis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manolaridis et al., 2018.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformer of the E211Q mutant ABCG2, cavity 2 is open to the extracellular side of the plasma membrane.
source: In the ATP-bound conformer of this mutant protein, cavity 1 is completely collapsed, the di-leucine gate is closed, while cavity 2 is open to the extracellular side of the plasma membrane (Manolaridis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manolaridis et al., 2018.

claim: Mutation of the catalytic glutamate may affect the energetics of conformational changes in ABC transporters.
source: However, mutation of the catalytic glutamate may affect the energetics of conformational changes in ABC transporters; thus, it may be argued that the OF state of the E211Q mutant ABCG2 observed in the presence of ATP does not represent a true catalytic intermediate (Manolaridis et al., 2018; Lusvarghi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Manolaridis et al., 2018 and Lusvarghi et al., 2021.

claim: ABCG2 and ABCG2-GFP were expressed at comparable levels in MDCK II cells.
source: ABCG2 and its N-terminally GFP-tagged variant (ABCG2-GFP) were expressed at comparable levels in MDCK II cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The transport activity of ABCG2 was not influenced by the GFP-tag.
source: In accordance with literature data (Orbán et al., 2008; Haider et al., 2011), the transport activity of ABCG2 was not influenced by the GFP-tag (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D and citations to Orbán et al., 2008 and Haider et al., 2011.

claim: ABCG2 inhibitors, such as Ko143, can enhance 5D3 mAb binding by shifting the equilibrium to the IF state.
source: Previous observations showed that ABCG2 inhibitors, such as Ko143, can enhance 5D3 mAb binding by shifting the equilibrium to the IF state (Ozvegy-Laczka et al., 2005; Telbisz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ozvegy-Laczka et al., 2005 and Telbisz et al., 2012.

claim: In the plasma membrane of untreated live cells, ABCG2-GFP and ABCG2 exhibited comparably low 5D3-reactivity, which was increased in a similar extent by Ko143 treatment.
source: Accordingly, in the plasma membrane of untreated live cells, ABCG2-GFP and ABCG2 exhibited comparably low 5D3-reactivity, which was increased in a similar extent by Ko143 treatment (Figure 2E–G), supporting the notion that the GFP-tag does not modify the conformational response of ABCG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The GFP-tag does not modify the conformational response of ABCG2.
source: Accordingly, in the plasma membrane of untreated live cells, ABCG2-GFP and ABCG2 exhibited comparably low 5D3-reactivity, which was increased in a similar extent by Ko143 treatment (Figure 2E–G), supporting the notion that the GFP-tag does not modify the conformational response of ABCG2.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable 5D3-reactivity data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Increasing ATP/Mg2+ concentrations gradually decreased the 5D3-A647-reactivity of ABCG2-positive cells, with practically zero staining at high ATP/Mg2+ concentrations.
source: In accordance with an ATP-regulated switch of the TMD conformation, increasing ATP/Mg2+ concentrations gradually decreased the 5D3-A647-reactivity of ABCG2-positive cells, with practically zero staining at high ATP/Mg2+ concentrations (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim state occurred in the absence of ATP hydrolysis when ATP was added without Mg2+ in the presence of EDTA.
source: To prevent nucleotide hydrolysis, ATP was either added in the absence of Mg2+ (ATP+EDTA; Figure 3C and D), on ice (Figure 3E and F), or ATP was replaced with the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP (Figure 3G and H). Interestingly, the conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim (i.e., 5D3 non-reactive) state also occurred in the absence of ATP hydrolysis and showed similar nucleotide concentration dependence (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-H and Table 1.

claim: The conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim state occurred in the absence of ATP hydrolysis when experiments were performed on ice.
source: To prevent nucleotide hydrolysis, ATP was either added in the absence of Mg2+ (ATP+EDTA; Figure 3C and D), on ice (Figure 3E and F), or ATP was replaced with the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP (Figure 3G and H). Interestingly, the conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim (i.e., 5D3 non-reactive) state also occurred in the absence of ATP hydrolysis and showed similar nucleotide concentration dependence (see Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F and Table 1.

claim: The conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim state occurred when ATP was replaced with the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP.

Interestingly, the conformational change driving ABCG2 into a 5D3-dim (i.e., 5D3 non-reactive) state also occurred in the absence of ATP hydrolysis and showed similar nucleotide concentration dependence (see Table 1).

claim: The 5D3-dim and 5D3-reactive conformations correspond to the OF and IF conformations as observed in ATP-bound and nucleotide-free crystal structures, respectively.
source: These results indicate that the 5D3-dim and 5D3-reactive conformations correspond to the OF and IF conformations as observed in ATP-bound and nucleotide-free crystal structures, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and comparison with structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Co-treatment with Vi or BeFx increased the apparent nucleotide affinity of ABCG2 about 10-fold in conditions permitting ATP hydrolysis.
source: Co-treatment with Vi or BeFx increased the apparent nucleotide affinity of ABCG2 about 10-fold (Table 1) in conditions permitting ATP hydrolysis (Figure 3A and B), confirming that both phosphate analogs can form stable ADP-trapped complexes with ABCG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Table 1.

claim: Both Vi and BeFx can form stable ADP-trapped complexes with ABCG2.
source: Co-treatment with Vi or BeFx increased the apparent nucleotide affinity of ABCG2 about 10-fold (Table 1) in conditions permitting ATP hydrolysis (Figure 3A and B), confirming that both phosphate analogs can form stable ADP-trapped complexes with ABCG2.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased apparent nucleotide affinity data shown in Figure 3A-B and Table 1.

claim: When ATP hydrolysis was prevented, the phosphate analogs Vi and BeFx did not have any effect on the KA values.
source: When ATP hydrolysis was prevented, the phosphate analogs did not have any effect on the KA values (Figure 3C–H and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-H and Table 1.

claim: ADP/Mg2+ could induce the IF to OF switch, albeit at slightly higher concentrations (KA = 7.38 ± 2.31 mM) compared to ATP/Mg2+.
source: Similar to the bacterial ABC transporter MsbA (Moeller et al., 2015), ADP/Mg2+ could also induce the IF to OF switch, albeit at slightly higher concentrations (KA = 7.38 ± 2.31 mM) compared to ATP/Mg2+ (see also Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and comparison with MsbA cited from Moeller et al., 2015.

claim: Nucleotide trapping occurred in the presence of phosphate analogs and ADP/Mg2+.
source: Moreover, nucleotide trapping occurred in the presence of phosphate analogs and ADP/Mg2+ (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: In the trapping reactions with ADP/Mg2+, about 30% of ABCG2 molecules remained in a 5D3-reactive state even in the presence of very high nucleotide concentrations.
source: However, in the trapping reactions with ADP/Mg2+, about 30% of ABCG2 molecules remained in a 5D3-reactive state even in the presence of very high nucleotide concentrations.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The ternary complex resulting from ADP/Mg2+ is different (i.e., less stable, possessing a shorter lifetime compared to the complex produced from ATP/Mg2+ in the hydrolytic cycle) and therefore the trapping reaction occurs with lower efficiency.
source: This observation may suggest that the ternary complex resulting from ADP/Mg2+ is different (i.e., less stable, possessing a shorter lifetime compared to the complex produced from ATP/Mg2+ in the hydrolytic cycle) and therefore the trapping reaction occurs with lower efficiency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that 30% of ABCG2 molecules remained 5D3-reactive with ADP/Mg2+.

claim: In energized cells, the cytosolic ATP concentration is more than 10-fold higher compared to ADP concentrations.
source: Since in energized cells the cytosolic ATP concentration is more than 10-fold higher compared to ADP concentrations (Williams et al., 1993), these results indicate that in live cells, (i) the switch from the 5D3-reactive IF to a 5D3-dim OF conformation is induced by ATP binding; and (ii) resetting to the 5D3-reactive IF conformation can only occur after the release of the hydrolysis products.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Williams et al., 1993.

claim: In live cells, the switch from the 5D3-reactive IF to a 5D3-dim OF conformation is induced by ATP binding.
source: Since in energized cells the cytosolic ATP concentration is more than 10-fold higher compared to ADP concentrations (Williams et al., 1993), these results indicate that in live cells, (i) the switch from the 5D3-reactive IF to a 5D3-dim OF conformation is induced by ATP binding; and (ii) resetting to the 5D3-reactive IF conformation can only occur after the release of the hydrolysis products.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and the knowledge that ATP concentrations are much higher than ADP in live cells.

claim: Resetting to the 5D3-reactive IF conformation can only occur after the release of the hydrolysis products.
source: Since in energized cells the cytosolic ATP concentration is more than 10-fold higher compared to ADP concentrations (Williams et al., 1993), these results indicate that in live cells, (i) the switch from the 5D3-reactive IF to a 5D3-dim OF conformation is induced by ATP binding; and (ii) resetting to the 5D3-reactive IF conformation can only occur after the release of the hydrolysis products.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Transported substrates increase the turnover rate of ATP hydrolysis in many ABC transporters including ABCB1 and ABCG2.
source: Transported substrates increase the turnover rate of ATP hydrolysis in many ABC transporters including ABCB1 and ABCG2 (Sarkadi et al., 1992; Telbisz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sarkadi et al., 1992 and Telbisz et al., 2012.

claim: The accumulation of ABCG2 in the Vi- or BeFx-trapped post-hydrolytic complex was accelerated by substrates.
source: Accordingly, the accumulation of ABCG2 in the Vi- or BeFx-trapped post-hydrolytic complex was accelerated by substrates (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: E3S and quercetin induced an about a fivefold increase in the rate of the trapping reaction.
source: E3S and quercetin induced an about a fivefold increase in the rate of the trapping reaction (for t1/2 values, see Figure 4B), which is consistent with the extent of stimulations achieved by these compounds in the ATPase assay (Telbisz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Telbisz et al., 2012.

claim: Trapping reactions starting from ADP/Mg2+ were not accelerated by quercetin or E3S.
source: Consistently, trapping reactions starting from ADP/Mg2+ were not accelerated by quercetin or E3S (Figure 4B), suggesting that substrates do not affect the overall stability or lifespan of the ADP-bound, phosphate analog-sensitive ABCG2 conformer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Substrates do not affect the overall stability or lifespan of the ADP-bound, phosphate analog-sensitive ABCG2 conformer.
source: Consistently, trapping reactions starting from ADP/Mg2+ were not accelerated by quercetin or E3S (Figure 4B), suggesting that substrates do not affect the overall stability or lifespan of the ADP-bound, phosphate analog-sensitive ABCG2 conformer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substrates did not accelerate trapping from ADP/Mg2+.

claim: ABCG2 molecules are intrinsically dynamic.
source: Under these conditions, we observed a gradual decrease of the 5D3-A647 fluorescence of cells, which was completely prevented by Ko143 treatment, supporting the notion that the ABCG2 molecules are intrinsically dynamic, while Ko143 stabilizes them in the IF 5D3-reactive conformation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of gradual decrease in 5D3-A647 fluorescence shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ko143 stabilizes ABCG2 molecules in the IF 5D3-reactive conformation.
source: Under these conditions, we observed a gradual decrease of the 5D3-A647 fluorescence of cells, which was completely prevented by Ko143 treatment, supporting the notion that the ABCG2 molecules are intrinsically dynamic, while Ko143 stabilizes them in the IF 5D3-reactive conformation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The dissociation rate of the 5D3 antibody was significantly enhanced in the presence of transported substrates or ATP/Mg2+.
source: The dissociation rate of the antibody was significantly enhanced in the presence of transported substrates or ATP/Mg2+ (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The largest (about fivefold) decrease of the t1/2 values corresponding to the half-life of the 5D3-bound ABCG2 conformer was observed when substrates were co-administered with ATP/Mg2+.
source: However, the largest (about fivefold) decrease of the t1/2 values corresponding to the half-life of the 5D3-bound ABCG2 conformer was observed when substrates were co-administered with ATP/Mg2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The time dependence of the AMP-PNP/Mg2+-induced 5D3 dissociation was comparable to that obtained with ATP/Mg2+.
source: The time dependence of the AMP-PNP/Mg2+-induced 5D3 dissociation was comparable to that obtained with ATP/Mg2+ supporting that the antibody dissociation kinetics observed either in the presence of ATP/Mg2+ or AMP-PNP/Mg2+ may reflect the first nucleotide-induced IF to OF transition of ABCG2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The antibody dissociation kinetics observed either in the presence of ATP/Mg2+ or AMP-PNP/Mg2+ may reflect the first nucleotide-induced IF to OF transition of ABCG2.
source: The time dependence of the AMP-PNP/Mg2+-induced 5D3 dissociation was comparable to that obtained with ATP/Mg2+ supporting that the antibody dissociation kinetics observed either in the presence of ATP/Mg2+ or AMP-PNP/Mg2+ may reflect the first nucleotide-induced IF to OF transition of ABCG2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable dissociation kinetics with ATP/Mg2+ and AMP-PNP/Mg2+.

claim: When co-administered with AMP-PNP/Mg2+, substrates did not increase further the dissociation rate of 5D3.
source: Strikingly, when co-administered with AMP-PNP/Mg2+, the same substrates did not increase further the dissociation rate of 5D3, suggesting that the NBD dimer formation induced by AMP-PNP/Mg2+ binding switches ABCG2 into the low drug binding affinity state (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The NBD dimer formation induced by AMP-PNP/Mg2+ binding switches ABCG2 into the low drug binding affinity state.
source: Strikingly, when co-administered with AMP-PNP/Mg2+, the same substrates did not increase further the dissociation rate of 5D3, suggesting that the NBD dimer formation induced by AMP-PNP/Mg2+ binding switches ABCG2 into the low drug binding affinity state (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that substrates did not further increase 5D3 dissociation with AMP-PNP/Mg2+.

claim: A similar decrease of the t1/2 values was observed when substrates were added before AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment.
source: However, a similar decrease of the t1/2 values was observed when substrates were added before AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment (compare Figure 5B and C), indicating that transition to the OF state can also be accelerated by substrates with AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Transition to the OF state can be accelerated by substrates with AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment.
source: However, a similar decrease of the t1/2 values was observed when substrates were added before AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment (compare Figure 5B and C), indicating that transition to the OF state can also be accelerated by substrates with AMP-PNP/Mg2+ treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Substrate binding at the TMDs induces a structural change in the transporter that can facilitate the nucleotide-dependent NBD dimer formation and the concomitant IF to OF transition.
